title: Salsa Roja
subtitle: Roasted tomato and chilli sauce
excerpt: Tomatoes and jalapeños charred under the grill, then blended with garlic and coriander into a deep, smoky red salsa. Far better than anything from a jar and ready in 20 minutes.
sourceNotes: Salsa roja (roasted tomato salsa): a Mexican and Tex-Mex cooked salsa made by charring tomatoes and chillies before blending. The charring gives the salsa a deeper flavour than raw or purely tinned versions. Based on classic Mexican and American Tex-Mex published sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in small portions for up to 3 months. Defrost in the fridge overnight.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and refrigerate; keeps for 5 days in the fridge. Good on tacos, enchiladas, quesadillas, or eggs.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves overnight as the flavours develop. Make ahead and refrigerate.

content.text: Salsa roja gets its depth from charring: tomatoes and jalapeños placed under a very hot grill until the skins blacken and the flesh collapses. The char adds bitterness and smoke that raw or tinned tomatoes alone can't provide. You want real char on the skin: actual blackened patches, not just darkened colour. Blend with the liquid from the tray; don't discard it.

items.prepNote: halved, seeds removed for a milder salsa

content.text: Heat the grill to its highest setting. Place the tomato halves (cut side up), jalapeños, garlic, and red onion wedges on a baking tray. Drizzle with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil and season with salt.
Grill for 15-20 minutes until the tomato skins are charred and collapsed and the jalapeños have blackened patches. The garlic should feel soft when pressed.
Leave to cool for 5 minutes. Peel and discard the garlic skins. Transfer everything from the tray, including all the cooking juices, to a blender. Add the coriander and lime juice.
Blend briefly: the salsa should be rough and textured, not a smooth purée. Taste and adjust with salt and lime juice.
If serving warm, heat in a small saucepan for a few minutes. Salsa roja is good warm or at room temperature.

items.symptom: Salsa is too smooth, more like passata
items.fix: Pulse the blender 3-4 times rather than running it continuously. A rough, chunky texture is traditional and tastes better than smooth.

items.cause: Under-seasoned, or coriander and lime missing
items.fix: Season generously with salt. The coriander and lime are not optional garnishes; they're core flavourings that lift the charred tomato base.

items.symptom: Too much liquid — more watery than saucy
items.cause: Tomatoes very juicy, or cooking juices over-diluted in the blend
items.fix: Heat the blended salsa in a small pan for 5 minutes to reduce and concentrate. Add a small pinch of sugar if the acidity is too sharp.

items.symptom: Garlic tastes raw in the final salsa
items.cause: Garlic not cooked long enough under the grill
items.fix: The garlic should feel completely soft and yielding when pressed after grilling. If still firm, return the baking tray to the grill for another 5 minutes.

content.text: Salsa roja is the most common cooked salsa in Mexican cooking. Charring tomatoes and chillies before blending is an ancient technique; molejetes (stone mortars) filled with charred vegetables appear in Mexican codices from before the Spanish conquest. The method gives a depth that no amount of tinned tomatoes can replicate. In Tex-Mex cooking, salsa roja is used as a table condiment, a cooking sauce for enchiladas, and a base for tortilla soup.
